solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Hangman and Beetle, say fine for relaxing times

indicators.note: something relaxing loosens its hold, so the word before it is let go and rearranged

blocks.note: the VW Beetle is an example of a car

explanation.surface: An executioner, together with a beetle, apparently imposes a penalty on idling.
explanation.walkthrough: CAR, rearranged FINE and X give CARNIFEX; 'and' and 'for' are glue that make the surface read.
explanation.definitionFit: A carnifex was the Roman public executioner, a literary word for a hangman.

clue.text: Direct answer accepted by broadcaster

indicators.note: what is accepted is taken in, so the broadcaster holds the other letter inside it

explanation.surface: A straight reply is taken on board by a TV channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direct' looks like an adjective meaning straight, matching 'answer', but it is a verb. Cann is a mostly Scots and nautical word found in Chambers.
explanation.definitionFit: To cann is to direct a ship's steering, conning or guiding its course.

clue.text: Strain to secure first of the Japanese porcelain

indicators.note: first of asks for only the opening letter of the following word
to secure something is to hold it fast, so the tune wraps round the letter

blocks.note: a strain is a melody, as is an aria

explanation.surface: A musical line is fastened to the start of a description of Japanese ceramics.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'Japanese' belongs to the definition, not the wordplay; only 'the' supplies a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Arita is a kind of porcelain named after the town in Japan where it is made, also called Imari ware.

clue.text: The rental's high leading to complaint

indicators.note: high here means intoxicated, and drunken words stagger into a new order

blocks.note: every letter of these words is used

explanation.surface: A steep rent provokes grumbling from a tenant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' looks like a grievance about the rent, but it is the medical sense of an ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: Nettle rash is urticaria, a skin ailment, and a complaint in the sense of a minor illness.

clue.text: Spot iron weapon emplacement overlooking Argentina

indicators.note: in a down entry, overlooking means sitting above, so the earlier parts come first

blocks.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
RA is Argentina's international vehicle registration code

explanation.surface: A gun position is sited above a sheet of iron somewhere in Argentina.
explanation.definitionFit: A fenestra is a small window-like opening, including a transparent spot on an insect's wing.

clue.text: Objects from old village fashionable no longer

indicators.note: what is no longer there has gone, so that word is dropped from the old term

blocks.note: an archaic word for a village or hamlet

explanation.surface: Artefacts from a historic village have fallen out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: ENDSHIP loses HIP. Endship is obsolete, found in Chambers.
explanation.definitionFit: Ends are aims or goals, the same sense as objects in 'the object of the exercise'.

clue.text: Butcher has ox tongue

indicators.note: to butcher something is to hack it about, so the letters are cut up and reset

explanation.surface: A butcher has ox tongue on sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butcher' and 'ox tongue' make a meat counter; tongue is really a language.
explanation.definitionFit: Xhosa is a Bantu language of South Africa, and tongue is a common synonym for language.

clue.text: Father's shunned breaks in outmoded resorts

indicators.note: someone shunned is kept out, so that word's letters are left out of the next

explanation.surface: Dad is left out of the holidays in old-fashioned seaside towns.
explanation.walkthrough: PAUSES without PA. 'Resorts' looks like a noun for holiday places, but here it is a verb, in an archaic sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Use once meant to frequent a place, so the obsolete verb uses matches resorts, as in 'resorts to the tavern'.

clue.text: Snatching mobile for bit of a lark could be the beginning of this

definitions.text: Snatching mobile for bit of a lark could be the beginning of this

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a single letter of it, here its opening one
for means in place of, so one letter is swapped in where the other stood

blocks.note: M is a standard abbreviation for mobile

explanation.surface: Grabbing someone's phone for a laugh might be how a gang robbery starts.
explanation.walkthrough: In STEALING the L is replaced by M. Read whole, the clue also describes the crime: one phone grab can begin a rush of thefts.
explanation.definitionFit: Steaming is British slang for a gang charging through a crowd or train robbing people as they go.

clue.text: English and French physicist in team

explanation.surface: An English scientist and a French one are on the same research team.
explanation.definitionFit: An écurie is a team of racing cars, from the French word for a stable.

clue.text: Snubbed tramp in traditional Indian dress is a hunter

indicators.note: snubbed is read as cut short, with its tip docked like a snub nose
in says that one piece sits inside the garment

blocks.note: a tramp is a long walk

explanation.surface: A vagrant dressed as an Indian woman is ignored, and turns out to be a hunter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tramp' looks like a vagrant but is a long walk, and 'snubbed' docks its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A shikaree, or shikari, is a big-game hunter in India, especially a native guide.

clue.text: Change of direction in a subject for French department

indicators.note: a change of direction swaps one compass-style side letter for its opposite

blocks.note: a liege is a vassal, one owing allegiance

explanation.surface: Changing course in a school subject to study French local government.
explanation.walkthrough: In A LIEGE the L (left) changes to R (right). Liege can mean either lord or vassal; here it is the subject.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ariège is a département in southern France on the Spanish border.

clue.text: Check after dangerous jog in the Highlands

indicators.note: after places the first named part behind the second one

blocks.note: as in a hot potato or radioactively hot
CH is the chess abbreviation for check

explanation.surface: A warning to check before a risky run in the Scottish hills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the Highlands' marks the word as Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotch is a Scots verb meaning to jog, jerk or fidget about.

clue.text: Refusal to admit Mean Machine for entertainment

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one word holds the other within it

explanation.surface: Someone declines to let the Mean Machine into the show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean Machine' reads as a nickname, but the two words split between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A Nintendo is a games console, a machine people play on for fun.

clue.text: I call up about theatrical angel getting money from southern Africa

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the phrase is read from bottom to top
theatrical suggests playacting and dramatic effect, so the word is staged in a new order
about means surrounding, so the reversed phrase goes round the other piece

blocks.note: to call someone something is to name them

explanation.surface: Someone phones a show's financial backer about money from Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Theatrical angel' looks like a set phrase, a backer of a show, but theatrical works alone on angel. EMANI goes round LANGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Emalangeni is the plural of lilangeni, the currency unit of Eswatini (Swaziland) in southern Africa.

clue.text: Force on record showing sign of emphasis

indicators.note: on places the first part next to the following one

blocks.note: to mark down is to record

explanation.surface: Emphasis on a record shows how it should be read.
explanation.definitionFit: A stress mark is the accent symbol used to show which syllable takes emphasis.

clue.text: Take supporter's banter

blocks.note: R stands for recipe, Latin for take, on prescriptions

explanation.surface: Accept a fan's teasing good-humouredly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take' is the R of prescriptions, from Latin recipe.
explanation.definitionFit: To rally someone is an older verb meaning to tease or chaff them, the same as to banter.

clue.text: Given out horn-call record, extremely disliked

blocks.note: to hate is to dislike extremely

explanation.surface: A hunting call was issued and recorded, but everyone hated it.
explanation.definitionFit: A recheat is a hunting-horn call recalling the hounds, so to rechate is to sound it.

clue.text: Heavy Metal article is what's prominent in the news

blocks.note: an item is an article, as in a list

explanation.surface: A piece about heavy metal music makes the headlines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavy Metal' looks like the rock genre; it is the dense element.
explanation.definitionFit: The lead item is the top story in a news bulletin or newspaper.

clue.text: Left university in old Greek city with depression

indicators.note: in places the paired letters inside the city's name

explanation.surface: A student quit university in ancient Greece, feeling low.
explanation.definitionFit: The blues is an idiom for low spirits or depression.

clue.text: Life peer's self-protection?

indicators.note: the possessive says the phrase has the answer, held within its letters

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A member of the House of Lords asks what defence they have.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by example: a sword for defending yourself. A life peer is a non-hereditary member of the House of Lords.
explanation.definitionFit: An épée is a fencing sword, the kind of weapon one might once have carried to protect oneself.

clue.text: Hitlerites liberated it? Ridiculous!

indicators.note: liberated means set free of, so the following pair of letters is released from the word
ridiculous means absurd or nonsensical, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: The idea of Nazis liberating anywhere is absurd.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove IT from HITLERITES and rearrange. Read whole, the clue mocks the thought: the Germans occupied St Helier, they did not free it.
explanation.definitionFit: St Helier is the capital of Jersey, occupied by German forces from 1940 and liberated in 1945.

clue.text: French city map despatched again with 50% missing

indicators.note: half missing means only one of the word's two halves is kept

explanation.surface: Half of a map of a French city went missing when it was posted again.
explanation.walkthrough: RESENT keeps only its first half.
explanation.definitionFit: Chartres is a cathedral city south-west of Paris.

clue.text: Dash found all around Arab capital

indicators.note: something found all around another encloses it on every side

blocks.note: Ar is an abbreviation for Arab or Arabic

explanation.surface: An Arab capital is discovered by someone racing round it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arab capital' reads as one phrase, but Arab is wordplay and capital alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Harare is the capital city of Zimbabwe.

clue.text: Queen's fashion knowing no bounds

indicators.note: having no bounds means its edges are gone, so the first and last letters go

blocks.note: a fashion is a way or manner of doing something

explanation.surface: A monarch's taste in clothes is extravagant.
explanation.walkthrough: MANNER loses its outer letters. 'Fashion' suggests clothing; here it is a way of doing things.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Anne reigned over Great Britain from 1702 to 1714.

clue.text: Figures turning up unchanged

indicators.note: a word that stays the same when turned upside down in a down entry reads alike both ways

explanation.surface: The numbers come out the same again.
explanation.definitionFit: Stats, short for statistics, are numerical figures.

clue.text: Dell is out of date for Scott's chum

indicators.note: is out of means a letter leaves the word and is no longer in it

blocks.note: a dingle is a wooded dell

explanation.surface: An old computer is obsolete, says a friend of a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dell is out of date' reads as a dig at the computer maker. Scott is Sir Walter Scott, who used the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingle is an obsolete word for a favourite or close companion, found in Scott's novels.

clue.text: Ancient swindle definitely set up? Only partly

indicators.note: only partly means just a portion of a word is used, sitting inside it
in a down entry, set up means placed upwards, so the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: letters three to seven of this word

explanation.surface: Was the old con definitely staged? Only to some extent.
explanation.definitionFit: To let in, in an old sense, is to cheat or trap someone, as in letting someone in for a loss.

clue.text: Upper-crust type Gray keeps short record: the art of dining

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the word loses its last letter
keeps means holds within, so the first pair of pieces holds the next

blocks.note: Gy is the symbol of the gray, the unit of absorbed radiation dose
a log is a written record

explanation.surface: A posh man named Gray keeps a brief diary of his dinners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gray' looks like a surname but is the unit of absorbed radiation dose, whose symbol is the two letters used here.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristology is the art or science of dining, a rare word coined in the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Sporting line of chemical engineer

blocks.note: o is a short form of of, as in o'clock

explanation.surface: An engineer's sporting background.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' reads as a line of work, but it is a marked line on the floor.
explanation.definitionFit: The oche is the line behind which a darts player must stand to throw.

clue.text: Endless bungling brings embarrassment

indicators.note: endless means without an ending, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a messy job is a bungled one

explanation.surface: Constant incompetence causes red faces.
explanation.definitionFit: A mess is an awkward predicament, and embarrassment can mean a difficult situation.

clue.text: Pointed adult cryptic clue upset

indicators.note: cryptic means puzzling or obscured, so the word is disguised by reordering its letters

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, as in film certificates
as in 'what's eating him?', ate means bothered

explanation.surface: A grown-up is put out by a sharp cryptic clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like another rearranging signal, but it is the past tense ATE, as something that troubled you ate at you.
explanation.definitionFit: Aculeate means sharp-pointed or prickly, and in insects having a sting.

clue.text: Establish ground in movie

indicators.note: in places the playing field within the film's title

blocks.note: a rec is a recreation ground

explanation.surface: Set up a location shoot for a film.
explanation.walkthrough: A rec is British slang for a public playing field.
explanation.definitionFit: To erect is to set up or found, as one establishes a building or institution.

clue.text: New name in Evangelical Union is showing lots of tedium

definitions.note: plural noun phrase, matching the plural answer

indicators.note: in sets the two letters inside the union's abbreviation

explanation.surface: A new name in a church union makes things boring.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is listless boredom, so ennuis are many bouts of tedium.

clue.text: Writing paper from Delaware belonging to me

explanation.surface: Stationery sent from Delaware that is mine.
explanation.definitionFit: Demy is a traditional size of paper, used for writing and printing.

clue.text: Meetings with US composer

blocks.note: first meaning: sittings of a body

explanation.surface: Gatherings attended by an American composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sessions are formal sittings of a court or council, and Roger Sessions was a twentieth-century American composer.
